subsection: 6. De Valera in power, Anglo-Irish relations and from Free State to Republic, 1932–1949

notes.b: The Cosgrave governments worked within the Commonwealth framework. Imperial conferences and the Statute of Westminster gave dominions greater independence, which de Valera later used.
points: The Imperial Conference of 1926 declared the dominions equal in status to Britain and independent within the Commonwealth, a principle commonly known as the Balfour Declaration.
The Statute of Westminster of 1931 removed most of the British Parliament's power to legislate for the dominions, and the Free State adopted it in its own terms later.
Cosgrave accepted the Treaty framework, the Governor-General and the oath, and his government saw the Commonwealth as the basis of the state's relationship with Britain.
Land annuities owed by Irish farmers under earlier land purchase acts were paid to the British Exchequer by the Free State in this period.

notes.h: Fianna Fáil's rise and the 1932 election
notes.b: Fianna Fáil's founding in 1926 and its entry into the Dáil in 1927 set up a challenge to Cosgrave's Treaty settlement, which de Valera won in 1932.
points: Fianna Fáil was founded on 16 May 1926 by de Valera, with the aim of ending the Treaty settlement through constitutional means.
The party entered the Dáil in August 1927 after its TDs took the oath as an ‘empty formula’, and it built support among small farmers and urban workers.
Fianna Fáil won 72 seats in the 1932 general election, and de Valera became President of the Executive Council with Labour's support in March 1932.
The new government's early measures included halting land annuity payments to Britain, with the oath's removal and the reduction of the Governor-General's role following in 1933 and 1936.

notes.b: De Valera used constitutional measures to remove the Treaty's symbolic and legal links with the Crown, a process completed in 1937 with a new constitution.
points: The Removal of the Oath Act of 1933 abolished the oath of allegiance to the King for members of the Oireachtas and for public servants.

The Constitution (Amendment No. 27) Act of 1936, known as the External Relations Act, removed the King's functions from Irish domestic affairs and allowed him to act on the state's behalf only for external matters.

The Abdication Crisis of December 1936 gave de Valera a chance to remove the King's functions, and the government used the External Relations Act to continue to treat the King as the head of the Commonwealth's external relations.
The Governor-General's role was reduced as the government took over his functions, and his office was not used in the new constitution.

notes.b: The Economic War was a trade conflict between Britain and the Irish state over the land annuities. Britain imposed duties on Irish agricultural exports, and the Free State answered with tariffs on British goods.
points: In 1932 de Valera withheld the land annuity payments, which the British government regarded as a breach of the Treaty.
Britain imposed special duties on Irish cattle, dairy and other agricultural exports, and the Free State responded with duties on British coal, cotton and other goods.
Irish cattle farmers suffered heavy losses, as Britain had been their main market, and the policy caused hardship in rural areas.
The Economic War encouraged Irish industrial protection, which Fianna Fáil used as a way of building manufacturing industry behind tariffs.

The Anglo-Irish Trade Agreement of 25 April 1938 ended the war: the land annuities were settled by a lump sum of £10 million, and the Treaty ports at Berehaven, Queenstown and Lough Swilly were returned to Irish control.

notes.h: The Blueshirts and the Constitution of 1937
notes.b: The Blueshirt movement of 1932–33 was a challenge from the right to de Valera's government, and the new constitution of 1937 set out a state with Catholic and nationalist emphasis.
points: The Army Comrades Association, later known as the Blueshirts, was formed in 1932 and led by former Garda Commissioner Eoin O'Duffy.
The movement was renamed the National Guard in 1933, and its members were absorbed into Fine Gael, the new party formed that year under Cosgrave.
Bunreacht na hÉireann was drafted by de Valera and submitted to a referendum on 1 July 1937, and it came into force on 29 December 1937.
Article 2 and Article 3 claimed the whole island of Ireland as the national territory, but they recognised the territorial limits of the state's laws until unity was achieved.
Article 41 described the family as the natural and fundamental unit of society and recognised the woman's role in the home.
Article 44 recognised the special position of the Catholic Church as the church professed by the majority of citizens; the article was later removed in 1972.
The new constitution created the office of President, and Douglas Hyde became the first President in June 1938.

notes.b: The inter-party government of John A. Costello declared Ireland a republic in 1948, which took effect in April 1949 and ended the Free State's links with the Commonwealth.
points: John A. Costello led the first inter-party government from February 1948, a coalition of Fine Gael, Labour, Clann na Poblachta, Clann na Talmhan and independent TDs.
The Republic of Ireland Act was passed in 1948 and came into force on 18 April 1949, Easter Monday, which ended the state's membership of the Commonwealth.
The Ireland Act of 1949, passed by the British Parliament, recognised the Republic and stated that Northern Ireland's constitutional position could not change without the consent of its parliament.
The Act ensured that Northern Ireland remained part of the United Kingdom, and it confirmed partition in law.

notes.h: Key personality: Éamon de Valera (part 2 and overall evaluation)
notes.b: De Valera dominated Irish politics for the period from 1932 to 1949 and was in power for most of it. Judgements about him depend on whether his constitutional settlement is judged a success or his economic and northern policies a failure.
points: He served as President of the Executive Council from 1932 and as Taoiseach from 1937 under the new constitution, and he was Taoiseach for most of the years to 1948.
He removed the oath, reduced the Governor-General's role to a near formality, and drafted the 1937 constitution, which remains the basis of the Irish state.
He negotiated the 1938 Anglo-Irish Trade Agreement, returning the Treaty ports to Ireland, and he kept the state neutral in the Second World War.
Contemporaries saw him as a unifying nationalist leader; opponents, including Cosgrave and the Blueshirts, saw him as dangerous and as a threat to the Treaty's settlement.
His policies failed to achieve Irish unity, and the Economic War damaged the rural economy, which critics regarded as costly failures.
Historians such as Tim Pat Coogan, in his 1993 biography, and Diarmaid Ferriter, in Judging Dev (2007), have judged him as an astute but controversial figure whose legacy is contested.

notes.h: Assessment: Cosgrave or de Valera in Anglo-Irish relations
notes.b: The two leaders pursued different routes: Cosgrave worked within the Commonwealth, while de Valera sought to reshape the link with Britain. Each left a different legacy.
points: Cosgrave's achievement was a stable relationship with Britain under the Treaty; his limit was that he left the oath, the Governor-General and the Treaty ports in place.
De Valera's achievement was the removal of the Treaty's main symbols and the 1938 settlement; his limit was that he did not reunify the island and his trade war cost farmers heavily.
Contemporary view: Fianna Fáil's supporters credited de Valera with achieving sovereignty, while Cosgrave's supporters saw his actions as a breach of the Treaty.

Later view: some historians argue that the Republic of 1949 was largely a legal change, because the state had been moving towards independence since 1922, while others credit de Valera's constitutional work with a real break from the Treaty.

keyTerms.definition: Supreme authority over a state's own affairs, which de Valera's government extended by removing the Treaty's symbolic and legal links with the Crown.
A state with no monarch at its head; Ireland became a republic in name in April 1949.
The status of a self-governing member of the Commonwealth, which the Free State held until it left the Commonwealth in 1949.
The formal loyalty owed to the Crown, which was removed from public life by the Removal of the Oath Act of 1933.
The 1931 Act that gave the dominions legislative independence from the British Parliament.
The 1936 Act that limited the King's functions to external matters and gave the state its own domestic constitutional arrangements.
The trade conflict between Britain and the Irish state from 1932 to 1938, arising from the withholding of the land annuities.
The Irish constitution, approved by referendum in July 1937 and in force from December 1937.
The movement formed in 1932 by supporters of the Cosgrave opposition, led by Eoin O'Duffy, which was absorbed into Fine Gael in 1933.
The 1948 Act that declared the state a republic and took it out of the Commonwealth, in force from 18 April 1949.
